prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat bands at the magic angle in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in moire quantum matter

statement.case_for: I opened with B034 (jamming) first and B022 second, but after reading the ballots I move B022 to the front of my own configuration. It is the only shortlisted candidate that six of eight members placed in their top three, and the scientific case is unusually clean: a quantitative continuum-model prediction of flat bands near 1.1 degrees (Bistritzer and MacDonald, 2011) followed by an unexpected experimental demonstration of correlated insulators and superconductivity in a single tunable carbon system (Jarillo-Herrero's group, 2018). Eight years on, the core observations have been reproduced across many groups, devices and materials (twisted TMDs and others), and the platform has become a laboratory for strongly correlated and topological phases. As someone who works on statistical physics of complex systems, I value that a clear control parameter, the twist angle, lets one tune through interacting phases. The theory-plus-experiment trio maps onto the credited names without any invented additions.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is maturity and attribution. The pairing mechanism and the nature of several correlated states are still debated, so a 2026 prize would reward a discovery whose interpretation is not settled. The first author of the decisive experimental papers, Yuan Cao, is not among the credited names, and other groups (Dean, Young, Yacoby, Efetov and others) and earlier moire band theorists (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto) have claims the three-person limit cannot accommodate. If the committee weights interpretive stability above breadth of impact, B036 is the safer choice.

responses.point: B022 is a nature-led surprise preceded by a sharp theoretical prediction, reproduced quickly, so early recognition is defensible; he also notes that Yuan Cao and other experimentalists fall outside the credited names.
responses.response: I agree with the reading of the discovery and with the view that rapid replication offsets the youth of the field. I would go one step further on the attribution problem than you do: the omission of Cao is not just a footnote, it is the main fairness risk in this configuration, and the committee should say openly that the citation honours the discovery and the prediction rather than every contributor. I also do not think the unsettled pairing mechanism is disqualifying, because the prize would rest on the existence of flat-band-driven correlated phases, not on a theory of the superconductivity.

responses.point: B036 (optical lattice clocks) is a clear, original and mature precision-measurement achievement with a clean two-person credit; she ranks B022 fourth partly because the superconductivity mechanism is unsettled and recognition could be premature by some years.
responses.response: Your maturity argument is the best case against my preferred option and I take it seriously. Where I differ is on how much weight the interpretive debate deserves: the clock result is more settled, but the overlap with the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize is real, and I ranked B036 fourth for that reason. Between a mature but incremental-looking metrology prize and a younger discovery that opened a new subfield, I lean to the latter, though I would accept B036 as a strong fallback if the committee decides B022 is premature. A redefinition of the second would strengthen your case materially.

responses.point: B054 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) reshaped band-structure classification around topology and has been confirmed in many materials, leaving room after the 2016 prize.
responses.response: I ranked B054 seventh and still hold that view. The conceptual contribution is deep, but the credited trio leaves out Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, who made the HgTe proposal that Molenkamp's experiment tested, and Zhang's death removes any chance of repairing that. With B022 the credited theory and experiment link directly. The 2016 overlap is a second concern for me, since the committee has already recognised topology in condensed matter once.

responses.point: B036 is atomic physics at its purest: the most precise measurement devices ever built, with consequences for the second, constants and geodesy, and recognition is arguably overdue.
responses.response: I accept that precision measurement belongs on the shortlist and I rank B036 as my first alternative. My reservation is the one you flag yourself: the comb lineage is already honoured, so the committee must decide the clock is a distinct discovery rather than a consequence of the comb. I would want that argued explicitly before choosing it over a candidate that opened a new field.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges the unresolved superconducting mechanism in magic-angle graphene to make the prize premature.
How to handle Yuan Cao and other experimental contributors who are outside the credited names.
Whether B034 (jamming), which only I ranked first, is a single discovery or a framework with contested universality; I therefore do not push it as the preferred configuration.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile: none of the credited candidates are listed among my documented co-authors, supervisors or institutional connections. My own research interest in statistical physics of complex systems is relevant to B034 and I note it for transparency, but it is a field affinity, not a personal connection.
